procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (convicted the appellant for five different offences)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 14, 1966, of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1971 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Allahabad High Court heard a criminal appeal (No. 1971 of 1964) against the trial court's decision. The High Court altered the conviction to one under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code and upheld the sentence of fine of Rs. 3,000/-. However, the Supreme Court noted errors in the High Court's judgment, specifically regarding the sentence in default of payment of fine and convicting the appellant for an offence he was not charged with.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the conviction under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code, and remitted the case to the High Court for rehearing the appeal and giving a decision on the appeal in respect of the offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code is set aside.
directions: The case will now go back to the High Court for re-hearing the appeal and giving a decision on the appeal in respect of the offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in convicting the appellant under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code when no charge for this offence was framed in the trial court.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a trial court for several offences, including conspiracy, cheating, and forgery.

On appeal, the High Court did not rule on the original charges. Instead, it substituted the conviction with a new one for abetting cheating by personation (section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code).
The basis for the High Court's new conviction was its finding that the appellant had wrongly identified a person before an Oath Commissioner, thereby abetting the creation of a false affidavit.
law: A person cannot be convicted of an offence for which no charge was framed in the trial court.
An accused must be questioned under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure about the evidence relating to the specific charge they face, to give them an opportunity to explain.

For an act to constitute the offence of 'cheating' under the Indian Penal Code, the deception must induce the person deceived to do something that causes, or is likely to cause, damage or harm to them in body, mind, reputation, or property.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court made a significant procedural error by convicting the appellant for an offence (s. 419/109) that was never charged in the trial court.

Compounding this error, the appellant was never questioned about or asked to explain the evidence related to the specific act of cheating the Oath Commissioner, which denied him a fair opportunity to defend himself against this new charge.

Furthermore, the Supreme Court analyzed the substance of the new conviction and found that the essential ingredients of 'cheating' were not met. The act of the Oath Commissioner attesting the affidavit, even if induced by the appellant's deception, was not likely to cause any damage or harm to the Oath Commissioner's body, mind, reputation, or property. Since the primary offence of cheating was not established, the conviction for abetting it could not stand.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred both procedurally and substantively. It was a procedural error to convict the appellant for an offence he was never charged with or given a chance to explain. It was a substantive error because the facts found by the High Court did not constitute the offence of cheating. Therefore, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's conviction, and sent the case back to the High Court to be reheard on the original charges from the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court failed to record a clear finding on whether the offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court were proven.

application: The Supreme Court observed that the High Court, in its judgment, did not examine the evidence relating to the specific offences for which the appellant had been convicted by the trial court.
The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had not recorded any findings on the facts which, according to the prosecution, constituted the commission of those original offences.
Instead of ruling on the original charges, the High Court had convicted the appellant for a different offence with which he had never been charged or tried.

The Supreme Court explicitly stated that in adopting this course, the High Court "failed to record a clear finding whether the offences, for which the appellant had been convicted by the trial Court, were proved or not."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had failed in its duty to decide the appeal in respect of the offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's conviction and remitted the case back to the High Court for a rehearing on the original charges.

issue.issue_text: Whether the facts found in the case constituted the offence of cheating.

facts: The appellant practiced deception by wrongly identifying a person before an Oath Commissioner.
This deception induced the Oath Commissioner to attest an affidavit, believing the person was someone else (Govind Ram).
law: The offense of cheating, as defined in section 415 of the Indian Penal Code, requires that the deception must induce the person deceived to do an act that causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
Alternatively, the deception must induce the person to deliver property or consent to the retention of property.
application: The Court analyzed the act performed by the Oath Commissioner (attesting the affidavit) and determined that this act could not possibly cause any damage or harm to him in body, mind, reputation, or property.
The Court also found that the Oath Commissioner was not induced to deliver any property to anyone or to consent that any person should retain any property.
reasoning.conclusion: Since a necessary ingredient of the offense of cheating—the element of causing or being likely to cause harm or damage to the person deceived—was not met by the facts, the Supreme Court concluded that the offense of cheating was not constituted at all.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence of two years' imprisonment in default of payment of fine, affirmed by the High Court, was illegal and in contravention of section 65 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The High Court altered the appellant's conviction to an offence under section 419 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
While altering the conviction, the High Court upheld the fine of Rs. 3,000/- but did not make a specific order about the imprisonment in default of payment.
The Supreme Court interpreted this as an implied affirmation of the trial court's original sentence of two years' imprisonment in default of payment.
law: Under section 419 of the IPC, the maximum sentence of imprisonment that can be awarded is three years.
Under section 65 of the IPC, the term of imprisonment in default of payment of a fine cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence.
application: The maximum permissible default sentence for an offence under section 419 IPC is one-fourth of the maximum imprisonment of three years.
The two-year (24 months) default sentence implicitly affirmed by the High Court was significantly longer than the legally permissible maximum of nine months.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the sentence of two years' imprisonment in default of payment of the fine was illegal and in contravention of section 65 of the IPC. This was because the High Court, after altering the conviction to an offence with a maximum punishment of three years, failed to reduce the default sentence to the legally permissible limit of nine months (one-fourth of three years).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for an offense for which an accused has not been charged or tried is invalid.
obiter: The term of imprisonment in default of payment of a fine cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment that can be awarded for the offense.
An appellate court must examine the evidence and record clear findings on the facts constituting the offenses for which an appellant was convicted by the trial court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court committed multiple serious errors by convicting the appellant for an offence (cheating) with which he had never been charged and for which he had never been tried, without giving him an opportunity to explain the evidence against him. Furthermore, the High Court failed in its appellate duty to examine the evidence and record a clear finding on whether the original offences for which the appellant was convicted by the trial court were actually proven.
legal_tests_applied: To constitute the offence of cheating, the following ingredients must be met: (i) There should be fraudulent or dishonest inducement of a person by deceiving him; (ii) (a) The person so deceived should be induced to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property; or (b) The person so deceived should be intentionally induced to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived: and (iii) In cases covered by (ii)(b), the act or omission should be one which causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property.

Under section 65 of the Indian Penal Code, the maximum term of imprisonment in default of payment of a fine cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment fixed for the offence. For an offence under section 419 I.P.C., where the maximum sentence is three years, the maximum default sentence is nine months.
policy_considerations: It is an extraordinary and improper course for an appellate court to convict an accused for an offence with which he had never been charged and for which he had never been tried.

An accused must be given an opportunity to explain the evidence relating to a charge against them, as required by procedural law (section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure), before a conviction can be sustained.

An appellate court has a duty to examine the evidence and record findings on the facts related to the offences for which the accused was convicted by the trial court, rather than ignoring them and substituting a new conviction.
